title: Singapore’s hottest tech stocks just lost about a quarter of their value in a month
dek: Singapore’s tech stocks just had their worst month of 2026: the sector index lost 17.3% in October, and today’s Asia-wide selloff is keeping the pressure on.
author: Ethan Koh
caption: Share prices on a trading screen.
body: ## October was ugly, and tech took the worst of it

The Straits Times Index lost 5.2% in October on a total-return basis. Tech did far worse. The sector index fell 17.3%, the worst of any sector that month. S-REITs, by comparison, barely flinched at 1.4%.
The chip and electronics names got hammered:

- AEM: down 24% for the month, still up 335% for the year
- UMS Integration: down 26%, still up 80%
- Frencken: down 23%, still up 47%
- PC Partner: down 22%, still up 211%
These stocks ran so hard in 2026 that even a drop like that leaves them well ahead.
## It started in America

Investors on Wall Street have been getting nervous about how much money is going into AI and when it will actually pay off. Alphabet dropped 12.6% in a single session late last month, and by Oct 30 Singapore’s chip-linked stocks were feeling it. AEM fell 8.6% that day. The STI only slipped 0.4% to 5,376.74, because the banks and the rest of the index cushioned the blow.

Then came this week’s US midterms. Democrats won big, and the market immediately started worrying about tighter rules for AI. Several winning candidates have promised to curb data centre construction. The fear is that fewer data centres means less demand for the chips and equipment behind them. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% overnight, its worst day since April 2025.

Asia caught the fallout this morning. Seoul was down almost 9% at one point, Taipei about 8% and Tokyo 7%. Singapore was off more than 1% in early trading, so we got off lighter than most. That’s not the same as being immune.
## Big money is leaving, small investors are staying

Institutions pulled a net S$1.55 billion out of Singapore stocks in October. Retail investors went the other way and bought S$1.65 billion, which takes their net buying to S$5.9 billion for the first ten months of the year.
After a run like AEM’s, big funds taking profits isn’t a shock. Whether retail investors are right to buy the dip is a different question, and nobody can answer it yet.
## So is this a crash?

Not on the business numbers so far. Electronics output is up 24.6% in the first nine months of the year, and manufacturing is up 9.8%. The factories are busy. What changed is how much investors are willing to pay for the stocks.

Three things to watch from here: the third-quarter earnings updates due this month, the US debate over AI regulation, and interest rates. If the results hold up, October may look like a reset after a huge run. If they don’t, it may have been the warm-up.
This is general information, not financial advice.
## Sources

title: Meet the coworker with no face
dek: A few years ago, “AI employee” sounded like a pitch from a sci-fi movie. Today it’s a line on the org chart.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: A robot at a laptop.
body: Take McKinsey. CEO Bob Sternfels said in January that the firm had added 25,000 AI agents, which it treats as digital employees, to a human workforce of about 40,000. Do the math and that’s roughly five software workers for every eight people on the payroll. And McKinsey isn’t a factory. It’s a firm that sells human judgment for a living.

This is a look at what AI employees actually are, where companies are putting them to work, why the results are still hard to prove, and what the rise of the AI workforce means for your career. If you’ve wondered whether this is hype or the real thing, the honest answer is a bit of both.
## One firm, 25,000 digital workers

Read that McKinsey number again. Sternfels has said the goal is for every one of the firm’s 40,000 people to have an AI agent working alongside them. That isn’t a pilot project in a corner of the business. It’s a plan for how the whole company runs.

McKinsey is the headline case, but it isn’t alone. Large companies in banking, retail, software and consulting are all trying versions of the same idea, and they’re no longer calling it an experiment. They call it hiring.
## What is an AI employee, and how is it different from a chatbot?

The old picture of workplace AI was a chatbot waiting for someone to type a question. AI employees, also called AI agents or digital workers, are different. Companies describe them as digital coworkers that act on their own, with their own identities, access permissions and responsibilities. You give one a goal, and it works through the tools it’s been given to get there: reading an inbox, updating a customer record, drafting a follow-up, flagging a problem for a human.
That’s basically what a new hire gets on day one.
## They get logins, just like you

The comparison to a human hire goes further than you’d expect. Companies are treating the first week of an AI agent like an onboarding. The advice floating around HR and IT teams is to give an agent clear guidelines, a defined role, limits on what it can touch, and someone to report to, the same as you would for a person.

There’s a practical reason. An agent with the wrong access can do real damage fast, just like a new employee who can see every file on the server. So the boring parts of employment, like permissions, oversight and accountability, are being rebuilt for software.
It also raises a question nobody has a good answer to yet. Somewhere right now, a manager is probably wondering who does the AI’s performance review.
## Why companies want AI employees in the first place

The pitch is simple, and it’s the same one every new technology makes. An AI agent works around the clock, doesn’t need a notice period, and can be copied. If a company needs ten more people for a busy season, hiring and training them takes months. Spinning up ten more agents can take an afternoon.
That’s the appeal for a finance chief. For a manager, the pitch is different: the boring part of the job, the part everyone keeps putting off, gets done without anyone having to ask.
Both pitches have some truth in them. Neither tells you what an agent does when something unusual happens, and that’s usually where the trouble starts.
## Where AI agents are actually working
Sales and marketing, mostly. One report on how teams are “hiring” AI employees put sales and marketing at the top of the list, at 26.1%, with customer support and operations close behind.

It makes sense when you look at the work. These jobs are full of repeated tasks: qualifying leads, sending follow-up emails, answering the same ten support questions, updating the same spreadsheet. Software never gets bored of any of that.
Typical jobs handed to AI agents right now include:

- Sorting and replying to routine customer support tickets
- Drafting and sending sales follow-ups
- Pulling reports and cleaning up data for operations teams
- Scheduling, reminders and other admin
## The hiring wave is just starting

The wave is still building. More than half of talent leaders at big companies said they planned to hire AI agents in 2026. That’s a striking thing to say about a category that barely existed in most job descriptions three years ago.
## The part nobody puts in the press release

Here’s where it gets awkward. Almost every large company is using AI in some form, but few can prove it’s paying off. Adoption is close to universal at the enterprise level, yet measurable returns are still rare. Plenty of businesses bought the shiny new teammate and aren’t sure what it’s actually delivering.
That gap between “we use AI” and “AI makes us money” is one of the biggest open questions in business right now. Until it closes, every AI workforce announcement deserves a second look.
## The squeeze on entry-level jobs

The people side is rougher. Stanford researchers tracking payroll data found that workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed jobs saw employment fall about 11% between late 2022 and June 2026, while employment in the least-exposed jobs grew about 10%. Their headline measure: young workers in the most exposed fields now hold about 19% fewer jobs than they would have if they’d kept pace with their less-exposed peers. Experienced workers in the same fields show no comparable gap.
The job postings tell a similar story. One analysis found that about 71% of AI-related openings at S&P 500 companies are senior roles, and only about 13% are open to junior candidates.
That’s a real problem, and it goes beyond fairness. Entry-level jobs are where people learn the work. If software takes the easy tasks, how does anyone become a senior person in ten years?
## What AI employees still can’t do

Agents are good at following a pattern. They struggle when the pattern breaks. Think of a customer who’s furious about something that isn’t covered in any policy, a client whose real problem isn’t the one written on the ticket, or a decision where two reasonable rules point in opposite directions. Those are the moments people realise a human is needed, and they’re exactly the moments an agent is most likely to get something wrong with total confidence.

There’s also the matter of context. A good employee knows the unwritten rules: which client is touchy, which deadline is real, which manager says yes but means no. An agent only knows what it has been told.
## Who’s responsible when an AI employee gets it wrong?

If an agent sends the wrong email, approves the wrong refund or shares a file with the wrong person, who answers for it? Not the software. The responsibility lands on a human, usually whoever set the agent up or the manager it reports to.

That’s why companies are building oversight into these roles from day one, with clear limits on what an agent can do alone and a person who signs off on the rest. It’s also why the people who will be most valuable in this new setup are the ones who can supervise: spot a mistake quickly and know when to step in.
## What to watch next

Three things will tell us whether this is a lasting change or another hype cycle. First, whether companies can finally show real returns from their AI spending. Second, whether entry-level hiring recovers or keeps shrinking. Third, whether the idea of managing a team that’s half human and half software becomes a normal job, or stays a headline.
## So are humans out?

Not quite. After a long stretch of cautious hiring, several of America’s biggest employers are adding people again, and they say human involvement is still essential. The work is shifting more than it’s disappearing. Instead of doing every task yourself, you’ll be the one deciding what the AI should do, checking its work and catching what it gets wrong.
McKinsey’s own numbers point the same way. The firm is adding agents, but it is also still employing tens of thousands of people.
## Sources

title: Jensen Huang affair: Nvidia CEO faces board probe over Alice Huang, Megaspeed and spy claims as Nvidia stock takes a hit
dek: On Sunday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, and the company’s board responded by launching an independent investigation into reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: An Nvidia office building.
body: The reporting points to Alice Huang, an executive tied to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer that U.S. authorities were already eyeing over AI chip exports. By Monday, November 9, 2026, Nvidia stock was sliding roughly 4% to 6% in premarket trading, a jolt for a company valued near $4.5 trillion.

Why does a private lapse become a market event? Because Nvidia is the engine room of the global AI boom, and Washington is in the middle of deciding how tightly to leash the flow of its best chips toward China. A founder under board scrutiny, with a congressional briefing already requested, hands investors a risk they have never had to price: what happens to Nvidia if Huang is not the one steering?

A word on sourcing before we dig in. Everything here comes from published reporting and company statements. The intelligence claims rest largely on anonymous U.S. officials, and none have been publicly proven.
## Key takeaways

- Huang told employees he was “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues.
- The board put independent directors and outside counsel in charge of the probe, while saying it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.
- U.S. intelligence reportedly concluded that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to gather information on Huang. Those are reported assessments, not courtroom findings.
- Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and says official inspections turned up no violations.
- Nvidia shares have shed about 13% since October 28, the last close before The New York Times’ first spy report, per Yahoo Finance.
- Huang stays on as CEO for now, and President Trump says he should.
## Jensen Huang’s apology memo and admission

Huang’s memo, sent to staff on Sunday, November 8, opens with a blunt apology. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote, adding that his actions hurt her and their children. He took full responsibility, pledged to cooperate with the board’s investigation, and closed with a line that read as both plea and promise: leading Nvidia is “the privilege of my life.”
### What the memo did and did not say

Notably, the memo kept names out of it. CNBC reports that Huang mentioned neither Megaspeed nor Alice Huang, though he did refer to the board’s inquiry into the national security concerns raised in news reports.

The admission also marks a sharp turn. Nvidia had earlier described Huang’s contacts with Alice Huang as ordinary customer interactions, with no sensitive trade secrets or national security information shared. According to The Hill, a company spokesperson first waved off the relationship report before the memo landed.
### The board’s statement
On Sunday afternoon, the board stepped in. Its statement said it was acting “in light of recent reporting” that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The shape of the probe:

- A committee of independent directors leads the work, backed by outside independent counsel.
- The board says it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but promises to examine all available information.
- No deadline and no committee roster have been made public.
One governance wrinkle is drawing eyebrows: unlike many of his tech peers, Huang is not chairman of Nvidia’s board, according to CNBC.
## Who is Alice Huang, and what is the Megaspeed connection?

Alice Huang, also reported as Huang Le, shows up in coverage as an executive tied to Megaspeed. The House Select Committee on China has labeled her a “publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset.” The New York Times describes a Chinese citizen with polished English and a wide network among senior chip-industry figures, and Bloomberg reports she helped set Megaspeed up. Some outlets call her a former executive. In the reporting reviewed here, she has not publicly responded.

U.S. intelligence reportedly concluded that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited her to collect information on Huang, and the Times says Trump administration policymakers received a memo on the subject last spring. Singapore’s government, for its part, says it has not looked into her alleged intelligence ties or her relationship with Huang.
### Megaspeed and the AI chip export-control question
Megaspeed was already on Washington’s radar long before the personal drama surfaced. Here is the tangled backstory:

- **The purchases.** Trade records cited in reports show a Megaspeed-linked Malaysian unit buying at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia technology between June 2024 and February 2026. Senator Tom Cotton and Representative Bill Huizenga cited more than $4.6 billion in an earlier letter.
- **The inspection.** U.S. officials reportedly found Nvidia equipment still sitting in boxes at a Malaysian data center, and the Commerce Department has reportedly been looking into Megaspeed.
- **The worry.** Lawmakers want to know whether chips reached Chinese customers in violation of U.S. export controls. Running chips remotely from outside China is a separate matter and not necessarily illegal.
- **The pushback.** Megaspeed says inspections by the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, Malaysia’s trade ministry and Nvidia found no evidence of illicit transfers. Nvidia says its own checks found Megaspeed legally qualified, with no signs of diversion, and denies any role in smuggling. The reporting does not accuse Nvidia itself of breaking export rules.
To be clear, neither the Commerce probe nor Singapore’s inquiry has publicly established that Megaspeed illegally diverted chips to China.
## Wall Street reaction and Nvidia stock impact

Nvidia shares slipped roughly 4% to 6% in premarket trading Monday, depending on the outlet and the minute. Yahoo Finance reported a 5.5% dip and called it the stock’s lowest level in seven months. At a 5% drop, Bloomberg put the damage near $225 billion in market value.

Two caveats before anyone panics or pounces. First, some of the slide predates the scandal: 24/7 Wall St. notes the stock fell 9.26% last Thursday for reasons unrelated to Huang, so Monday blends sector jitters with leadership worries. Second, not everyone fell. Taiwan’s stock index climbed 4.9%, TSMC gained 4.7%, and AMD reportedly rose about 4% while Nvidia sank.
### The key-person risk

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives called the episode a “black eye” for Huang and framed the investor question bluntly: will he remain CEO? Ives expects Huang to stay on without interruption for now, but concedes there is real risk of removal depending on what the board uncovers. Huang himself owns about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, roughly 3.58% of the company, per its 2026 proxy statement.

History offers a loose compass at best. A 2018 study in the Journal of Financial Economics found stocks fell about 4% on average when the CEO was the one caught, as Yahoo Finance noted. But Nvidia dwarfs every company in that sample, so treat the precedent as a rough guide, not a forecast.
### Congress moves in

The political heat is rising, too. Three Republican House committee chairs have asked Huang for a joint closed-door briefing on November 18, while Democratic lawmakers separately want an investigation or testimony. CNBC reports Democrats are likely to press on whether the administration knew about the relationship and whether Huang swayed American policy, a question raised by Sam Bresnick of Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
## Industry and political reactions: leadership versus national security
Early reactions split along a familiar fault line: Huang’s value to Nvidia on one side, the security questions around him on the other.

- **The White House.** President Trump called Huang a “fine person.” Asked whether he should remain CEO, he said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure,” while noting he had not spoken with Huang about it.
- **The industry.** Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy argued that Huang’s concentrated power is why Nvidia moves faster than anyone, a strength that turns thorny when the person holding it is under review. One investor close to Huang told CNBC that, depending on the findings, a leave of absence is conceivable.
- **The China hawks.** Lawmakers pushing for tighter chip controls, including the Chip Security Act, which would require location checks on export-controlled AI chips, are likely to read the episode as ammunition.
Resolving that tension will not be quick. Huang is simultaneously Nvidia’s strategic engine and, in the current reporting, the figure at the heart of an alleged intelligence operation.
## What investors and Nvidia should expect next

The nearest landmark is November 18, the requested closed-door congressional briefing. After that, the road gets foggy: the board’s investigation has no announced deadline, so uncertainty is the base case, not the exception.
Keep an eye on four things:

1. **How far the board looks.** Whether it stays on the relationship or widens to Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed.
2. **Export-control enforcement.** Any Commerce Department move on Megaspeed, or traction for chip location-verification legislation.
3. **Governance shake-ups.** Any change to Huang’s role, an interim arrangement, or a push to split the chairman and CEO jobs.
4. **Customer and partner mood.** Whether big buyers and Asian suppliers keep seeing this as a leadership story rather than a supply story.

Nvidia’s products and balance sheet are not what the board is examining. Its founder is, and the market is now pricing a risk it has never carried. Be wary of knee-jerk price swings while the facts, especially the intelligence claims, are still being pieced together. This article is news analysis, not investment advice.

Figures reflect reporting as of November 9, 2026, and may change.
